name: Economics: Forecasting US unemployment with FRED-MD
description: Forecast the change in the US unemployment rate 1, 6 and 12 months ahead from the 126-series FRED-MD panel available at each month-end origin from 1990 to 2023. The evaluator recomputes the targets and scores the root-mean-square error relative to a direct autoregressive benchmark with BIC lag selection.

sources.locator: Stock and Watson (2002): forecasting US macroeconomic series with diffusion indexes (principal components of many predictors), direct multi-step forecasts and comparison with autoregressions.
McCracken and Ng (2016): the FRED-MD monthly database, its 128 (here 126) series and transformation codes.

FRED-MD databases page of the St. Louis Fed; the 2024-09 vintage (current.csv as archived on 2024-10-29, byte-identical to the official 2024-09.csv; data to 2024-08) is pinned in catalog/finance-data-lock.json.

requirements.datasets: FRED-MD 2024-09 vintage (the monthly file as archived on 2024-10-29) fetched by scripts/prepare_finance.py from a pinned Internet Archive snapshot and verified by SHA-256; not redistributed.

evaluation.benchmark: Economics: Forecasting US unemployment with FRED-MD
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: forecast_target(history, horizons) -> array of 3 floats: forecasts of the task's target 1, 6 and 12 months after the origin (horizons = [1, 6, 12]). Targets: for INDPRO and CPIAUCSL the annualized average growth 1200/h * ln(x_{t+h}/x_t) (percent per year); for UNRATE the change u_{t+h} - u_t (percentage points). history = {'yyyymm': (T,) ints, 'series': list of the 126 FRED-MD mnemonics, 'tcodes': (126,) McCracken-Ng transformation codes, 'panel': (T, 126) raw levels from 1959-01 through the origin month (NaN = missing), 'target': mnemonic, 'target_kind': 'growth' or 'difference'}. Called at the 404 month-end origins 1990-01..2023-08 of the 2024-09 vintage (pseudo-real-time); |forecast| <= 1000. Score: mean over horizons of RMSE(candidate) / RMSE(direct autoregression with BIC lag order 0-6 estimated from 1960), excluding forecasts whose target window includes 2020-03..2020-12 (minimize; the autoregressive seed scores exactly 1). The candidate runs in a separate sandboxed process: numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and the other installed packages are importable, while the evaluator's library, its data files, the network and subprocesses are not accessible; one thread and 3 GB of memory. It receives only the arguments described here, one call at a time: the arguments of a call are sent after the value of the previous call has been received. Arguments and return values travel as numbers, strings, lists, dicts with string keys and numeric numpy arrays, so a tuple arrives as a list

limitations: A single data vintage (2024-09, data to 2024-08) is used as if it were available in real time: data revisions and publication lags (ragged edges) of the 126 series are ignored, so forecasts are pseudo-out-of-sample.
Forecasts whose target window includes March-December 2020 are excluded from the RMSE; the pandemic months would otherwise dominate the comparison. The 2021-2023 inflation episode is included.

The evaluation period is public; a candidate that reads the prepared file or is tuned on 1990-2024 can look ahead. RMSE ratios near 1 have wide sampling uncertainty (overlapping multi-step forecasts); per-horizon Diebold-Mariano p-values are reported.

The candidate runs in a sandboxed child process that never receives later data, realised outcomes or reference solutions, and no statement of the candidate is executed in the evaluator's process; outside macOS (kernel sandbox) deliberately hostile native code could bypass the file policy.

state_of_the_art.statement: No published value exists for this local protocol. Local references (mean RMSE ratio to the autoregressive benchmark): four-factor diffusion index 1.008, its equal-weight combination with the benchmark 0.969.

science_relevance.scientific_problem: Forecast key macroeconomic aggregates out of sample using information from many predictors.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Forecasts of output, inflation and unemployment guide monetary and fiscal policy; whether large panels of predictors improve on simple autoregressions out of sample is a central question in empirical macroeconomics.

papers.title: Macroeconomic Forecasting Using Diffusion Indexes
papers.primary_goal: Forecast US macroeconomic time series using principal-component factors estimated from a large number of predictors.
papers.task_relation: The task forecasts the change in the unemployment rate from a large monthly panel of real-activity, price and financial series.

papers.title: Forecasting Using Principal Components From a Large Number of Predictors
papers.primary_goal: Develop and justify forecasting with principal components of many predictors.
papers.task_relation: Factor-based forecasts of this kind are natural candidates and local references.

science_relevance.reason: Both papers have macroeconomic forecasting with many predictors as their main research goal.
